title: The Fox and the Horse
paragraphs: A farmer had a horse that had served him loyally and well for years. Now the horse was too old to work, so the farmer stopped feeding him. “I don’t need you anymore,” he said. “Get out of my stable. I won’t take you back until you’re stronger than a lion.” Then he opened the door and drove him out.

The poor horse was miserable. He wandered through the woods, looking for a bit of shelter from the cold wind and rain. Before long a fox met him. “What’s wrong, my friend?” he asked. “Why are you hanging your head and looking so lonely and sorry for yourself?” “Ah,” said the horse, “justice and greed never live under one roof. My master has forgotten everything I did for him all these years, and now that I can’t work anymore, he has thrown me out. He says he won’t take me back unless I become stronger than a lion. How could I ever manage that? He knows I can’t, or he wouldn’t say such a thing.”

The fox told him to cheer up. “I’ll help you,” he said. “Lie down over there, stretch out stiff, and play dead.” The horse did as he was told. The fox went straight to the lion, who lived in a cave nearby, and said, “There’s a dead horse lying not far from here. Come along with me, and you can make a fine meal of him.” The lion was delighted and set off at once. When they reached the horse, the fox said, “You won’t be able to eat him in comfort here. Here’s what we’ll do: I’ll tie you tight to his tail, and then you can drag him to your den and eat him whenever you like.”

The lion liked this idea and lay down quietly so the fox could fasten him to the horse. But the fox tied the lion’s legs together as well, and he knotted everything so tightly that the lion, for all his strength, could not get loose. When the job was done, the fox slapped the horse on the shoulder and cried, “Giddy-up, Dobbin! Giddy-up!” The horse jumped to his feet and trotted off with the lion dragging behind him. The lion began to roar and bellow until every bird in the forest flew off in fright. But the horse let him bellow and walked calmly across the fields to his master’s house.

“Here he is, master,” he said. “I’ve beaten him.” When the farmer saw his old servant, his heart softened. “You shall stay in your stable,” he said, “and be well looked after.” And so the poor old horse had plenty to eat and lived on until he died.
